item.title: Parking supervision, three decisions it informs
item.description:
In short:

  1. Supervision provides a continuous measure of occupancy, where knowledge usually rests on occasional counts.
  2. That measure informs three distinct decisions: pricing, the direction of enforcement and arbitration over use of the roadway.
  3. Measurement technologies differ in accuracy and maintenance cost, and do not answer the same need.
  4. Occupancy data is not personal data, unlike payment and enforcement data linked to an identifiable vehicle.

What measurement replaces

Without instrumentation, an authority knows its parking through counts carried out a few days a year. Those surveys give a snapshot, not a trend, and by construction they miss exceptional situations.

item.title: Why online procedures at town halls plateau
item.description:
In short:

  1. Digitising a form does not digitise the processing it triggers: if that stays manual, the delay does not move.
  2. An online procedure with no quick answer adds a channel instead of removing one, because the user calls back or visits.
  3. The order of digitisation matters: start with high-volume procedures that have standardised processing.
  4. The useful indicator is the share of cases completed without further contact, not the number of forms opened.

The first factor: the processing behind

An online procedure has two halves. The first is visible: the form. The second is not: the handling of the case by a member of staff. Digitisation most often covers the first only.

item.title: Connected street lighting, two gains to separate
item.description:
In short:

  1. Remote management acts on two distinct items: electricity consumption and the organisation of maintenance.
  2. Dimming in the middle of the night is the most direct consumption lever.
  3. Maintenance shifts from systematic replacement to intervention on reported faults.
  4. An often underestimated side effect is obtaining an up-to-date inventory of the estate, rarely available at the start.

The two items concerned

Connected street lighting designates an estate whose light points can be controlled and report their state. The expected gains follow two different logics, better examined separately.

item.title: Managing public building retrofit with data
item.description:
In short:

  1. Instrumenting before deciding makes it possible to rank works on actual rather than theoretical consumption.
  2. Part of the consumption gap comes from settings and usage patterns, and can therefore be closed without heavy works.
  3. Starting with the highest-consuming and most heavily used buildings gives the best information at the lowest cost.
  4. Measurement remains useful after the works, to verify that the expected effect is observed.

Why measure before deciding

A public building estate is heterogeneous: schools, sports halls, offices, sometimes listed buildings. Decisions on works often rest on theoretical assessments, which describe what the building ought to consume.

item.title: How to choose a territorial data platform
item.description:
In short:

  1. A territorial data platform is a normalisation layer between sources and uses, not a dashboard.
  2. The data model and its conformity to an open standard determine the ability to change supplier later.
  3. Reversibility must be written into the contract, with a full documented export, not merely mentioned.
  4. The cost to compare is the total cost over time, including licences, scaling and ongoing operational maintenance.

The real role of the platform

The territorial data platform occupies an intermediate position. Upstream, the sources: sensors, business applications, files deposited by departments. Downstream, the uses: dashboards, applications for staff, publication to the public.

item.title: What urban hypervision is actually for
item.description:
In short:

  1. Hypervision aggregates the flows of several business systems into a single interface, without replacing them.
  2. It differs from supervision, which manages a single domain in detail and at a higher level of granularity.
  3. Its relevance depends on the number of systems to cross-reference, and therefore on scale: it is easier to justify across an inter-municipal body than in an isolated municipality.
  4. Its value is measured by the number of decisions it speeds up, not by the number of indicators displayed.

What hypervision does

A local authority rarely runs a single piece of software. It runs a dozen, bought at different times, from different suppliers, each with its own interface. Urban hypervision sits above that estate and offers a common reading of it.

item.title: What is a smart territory?
item.description:
In short:

  1. A smart territory is not a technology but an organisation: data produced by services, normalised, then returned as operational uses.
  2. The term is broader than smart city, because it includes inter-municipal bodies and sparsely populated areas, where pooling is the point.
  3. Projects that hold up start from an existing operational need, not from a procurement exercise for tooling.
  4. The main limit is organisational rather than technical: without a department that takes ownership of the data, the platform goes unused.

What the notion covers

The expression smart territory designates a local authority that steers its services from the data it already produces. Street lighting, building consumption, water levels, parking, requests received at the counter: each of these areas generates information, most often locked inside a separate business application.

item.title: About
item.description:
What Territoire Connecté covers

Territoire Connecté is a blog about the digital transformation of local government. The subject is usually covered either in purely technical terms or in purely institutional ones. The aim here is to hold both ends: explaining how the tools work, and which concrete decisions they actually support for a municipality, an inter-municipal body or a county.

item.title: Contact
item.description:
Writing to the editorial team

Territoire Connecté welcomes factual corrections, topic suggestions and field feedback from local authorities.

Particularly useful:

  • Factual corrections on a published article, with the source that settles the point
  • Field feedback from authorities on a data platform, connected lighting or digitisation project
  • Open datasets that are little known and usable on the themes covered here

Before writing

For a correction, give the URL of the article concerned and the passage in question. For a topic suggestion, one paragraph is enough: the context, the question raised, and what is missing from what already exists.
